raw_response.country: Global / multi-country (illustrative secondary examples from South Africa, Bolivia, Guinea, Ghana and other global South countries)

criterion_notes.c1: Touches on household and community water and sanitation service access (municipal privatization, prepaid meters, affordability, and disconnections in the global South) as framing and illustrative examples, although the primary analytical object is global water policy formation.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it examines governance, institutional, and policy factors (World Bank/IMF structural adjustment and PRSP conditionalities, transnational water policy networks, and public-to-private utility shifts). However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because its central analytical focus is macro-governance ideology and elite transnational policy networking ('green neoliberalism' and global policy forums such as the WWC, WCW, and WBCSD), rather than investigating how a specific rule-type mechanism directly governs household or community service access (tariff hikes, prepaid meters, and contract redefinitions are cited only in brief secondary vignettes). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded due to lack of empirical methods/evidence on service access (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude).
criterion_notes.c3: Critical political-economy essay and narrative policy overview with no reported empirical methodology, no sampling or research design, and no systematic empirical synthesis. Figures on water cutoffs, tariffs, and privatization contracts are cited from secondary NGO, journalistic, and scholarly reports (with only passing footnotes to August 2002 Johannesburg/Orange Farm visit notes and no methodological apparatus), warranting exclusion under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: The analytical outcome examined by the paper is how neoliberal 'Water for All' privatization policy achieved global discursive hegemony; household water cutoffs, tariff increases, and inactive connections appear only as secondary illustrative anecdotes rather than empirically measured study outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Does not report an identifiable empirical study design, a defined study population or sample, or an operationalized exposure-outcome analysis of service access.

evidence_quotes.quote: Three hundred thousand people in Alex are jammed into just over two square miles of land without access to aﬀordable clean water, electricity, safe housing, or basic sanitation services.
This article explains how this new global water policy became constituted so quickly, dispersed so widely, with such profound institutional eﬀects.
Below, I will explain this notion of green neoliberalism and how it has become the World Bank’s latest development regime over the past two decades
Given these realities, it is hard to believe that the shift from public to private providers has increased water access for the poor.

This article focused on the remarkable rise and legitimacy since the mid-1990s of powerful transnational networks promoting global water reform in order to help shed light on the increasingly signiﬁcant phenomenon of this type of elite policy networking

raw_response.exposure: World Bank and IMF water privatization campaign, loan conditionalities, and transnational water policy networks (macro-governance discourse)
raw_response.outcome: Global discursive hegemony of neoliberal water privatization policy (with secondary illustrative references to tariff increases and water cutoffs)
raw_response.rationale: Goldman (2007) is a critical political-economy and historical policy essay tracing how the World Bank and elite transnational policy networks (such as the World Water Council, World Commission on Water, WBCSD, and WaterAid) constituted and diffused a global 'green neoliberal' water privatization agenda. It contains no empirical methods section, no defined population or sample, no identifiable empirical study design, and no primary empirical evaluation or systematic synthesis of household or community water/sanitation service access (relying on secondary NGO/media citations and brief unmethodologized footnotes from the 2002 Johannesburg summit). In addition, its core focus is macro-governance and transnational policy-network hegemony rather than a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing household service access. Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence); it would also be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2 for failing Criteria 3, 4, and 5.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative policy and political-economy essay / critical commentary (no empirical study design reported)
